html:
An Egyptian Islamic scholar, judge and reformer, born in a village of the Nile Delta, who argued that Islam, rightly understood, agrees with reason and modern science. He was a leading thinker of the Nahda, the Arab cultural revival.

He studied and then taught at al-Azhar in Cairo. There he fell under the influence of the wandering activist Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, who preached that Muslims must unite and reform to resist European power. Abduh backed the Urabi revolt against foreign control, and after the British occupied Egypt in 1882 he was exiled. In Paris he and al-Afghani put out a journal, al-Urwa al-Wuthqa, read across the Muslim world.

Allowed home, he worked inside the system. He became a judge and in 1899 Grand Mufti of Egypt, the country's top religious legal officer. He pushed to reform al-Azhar's teaching, the religious courts and education. He held that Muslims should not just follow past scholars blindly but return to the Quran and early sources and think for themselves.

His ideas, known as Islamic modernism, were carried on by his student Rashid Rida. They fed both liberal reformers and, by another path, later Islamist movements.
